title: Design Systems at Scale
subtitle: First steps towards a unified platform

slides.title: Design Systems at Scale
slides.standfirst: Building the case for design systems across two enterprise product portfolios — then building the foundations. The inventory came first, the system second, and the buy-in came from arithmetic rather than from taste.

bullets.text: Principal UX Designer and Design Systems Lead
62 shades of grey, 16 button types, 5 icon libraries
A multi-day process reduced to under an hour

slides.notes: Lead with the inventory numbers. They do the persuading, and they are the only part of this story a CFO can act on.

slides.title: Products sold as a single platform were not built as one

bullets.text: Each had its own colours, type styles, icon families and component patterns.
There was no modular frontend architecture to categorise them against.
Two similar icons assigned to different actions. Two different icons assigned to the same action.
Products outside the core codebase received no updates at all when shared elements changed.

callout.text: For the organisation: slower delivery and duplicated engineering hours. For users: a platform that behaved like several unrelated applications.

slides.notes: The two-icons-one-action problem is the one that lands with engineers. It is a correctness bug, not a style preference.

slides.title: A platform of many products
slides.standfirst: The scale is the reason inconsistency compounds. Every new product added its own vocabulary, and nothing existed to make that expensive.

bullets.text: Adding a single new icon required a multi-day manual round trip, from artistic design through to codebase.
Which means the friction fell on exactly the act you most want to be cheap.
So teams routed around it — with their own icons, in their own files.

items.alt: The breadth of products in the platform
items.label: The portfolio

slides.notes: Explain the causal loop: high cost to contribute produces local workarounds, which produce the inconsistency that makes contribution expensive.

slides.title: The inventory, before the system
slides.standfirst: You cannot argue for a design system with an opinion. You can argue for one with a count.
slides.notes: This is the methodological claim of the whole case study. Say it plainly and it frames everything after.

slides.title: Walking the interface, and traversing the code
slides.standfirst: Six inventories built by hand: UI, patterns, colour, typography, icons and spacing — assembled by using the products and then reading the CSS and code files behind them.

slides.title: Design systems fail at the buy-in stage, not the craft stage
slides.standfirst: Inconsistency is a designer-legible problem. It had to become a finance-legible one.

bullets.text: Inventory findings quantified as development hours, then hours multiplied by average salary.
An impact map consolidating the findings into one argument.
A clear yes, from both the team and stakeholders.

callout.text: Sustaining the system after approval — governance that survives contribution from every designer and developer, and distribution that actually reaches teams outside the core codebase.

slides.notes: Hours multiplied by average salary is the whole trick. It converts an aesthetic complaint into a line item.

slides.title: Then the system — rules first, elements second
slides.notes: Order matters again. Teams that start with a colour palette and no governance produce a style guide that decays in a year.

slides.title: Decide the rules before drawing anything

bullets.text: Build from scratch, or adopt an existing product as the foundation?
How the system reaches teams — decided up front, not after.
System KPIs defined, so "is it working" had an answer.
A multidisciplinary design systems team with defined roles.
A decision-making process and a sprint cadence, with retrospectives.
Kactus, so design files behaved like source.

slides.title: Days, to under an hour
slides.standfirst: The icon pipeline was taken over end to end and automated, so any team member could add an icon to the platform themselves.

from.label: Separate icon libraries
from.note: Each with its own conventions and no shared updates

to.label: One shared library
to.note: Any team member can add an icon in under an hour

figure.caption: Five to one, and multi-day to sub-hour

slides.notes: This is the metric that made the system credible internally. It made contributing cheaper than routing around, which is the only durable defence a system has.

slides.title: A system only counts once other teams get updates without asking
slides.standfirst: Products outside the core codebase had been receiving nothing. Their legacy CSS and SVG files were migrated into the core codebase, so shared changes reached them instantly.

bullets.text: Legacy CSS and SVG pulled onto the shared library.
Updates arrive automatically rather than being reimplemented per product.
The complete CSO component library built in Figma.
Additional designers onboarded to own the icon pipeline.

figure.caption: After migration: one change, every product

slides.notes: Onboarding others to own the pipeline is the part most design system leads skip. A system that depends on one person is a bottleneck with documentation.

slides.title: Three things beyond the craft

cards.title: Count before you argue
cards.text: 62 greys and 16 button types are unarguable. Translated into hours and salary, they became a business case rather than a design opinion.

cards.title: Make contributing cheaper than avoiding
cards.text: A multi-day icon process guarantees local workarounds. Sub-hour contribution removes the incentive to fork.

cards.title: Solve distribution or don't bother
cards.text: A system that only serves the core codebase is a style guide. Migrating legacy CSS and SVG in is what made it a system.

slides.notes: These three are the transferable content. Anyone starting a design system should leave with them.

slides.title: The hard part of a design system is organisational, and it never stops being organisational
slides.standfirst: The palette, the scale and the components are the tractable half. Getting the yes, then keeping governance alive through contribution from every designer and developer, is the work that determines whether any of it survives.

callout.text: When a shared element changes, does every product get it without anyone filing a ticket? If not, you have a library that some teams happen to use.

slides.notes: End on the test. It is the same shape as the repository test in the research ops story — accumulation only counts if it is automatic.
